before-code.name: Architecture
before-code.tagline: Nine years in architecture and construction.
before-code.summary:
I began working professionally as an architect in my second year of college. Over the next nine years, I designed projects, coordinated with engineers and contractors, and led teams through work that had to stay within budget and schedule. At Mutaa Al-Hashimi, I designed more than 65 projects. At UNOPS in Anbar, I worked on a housing reconstruction program covering around 1,500 homes.

Along the way, I started writing Python and Dynamo scripts to automate repetitive work. That interest eventually led me to a career in software. The buildings below are part of that story, as is the way I work with a team today.

sections.heading: Working on buildings
sections.body:
My early work included studying and interning, a parking structure modelled in Revit, and learning from the documents and tenders for the new Central Bank of Iraq headquarters. At Al-Riyad Group, I worked on a modular showroom system that was used across nine showrooms.

At Mutaa Al-Hashimi, I managed and delivered more than 65 projects and led three architects through more than twenty projects. Later, at UNOPS, I led four architects and six engineers on the Anbar reconstruction program. Alongside the drawings and models, I was working with contractors, budgets and delivery schedules. Those responsibilities taught me to keep the plan clear and deal with problems before they held up the people doing the work.

sections.heading: Finding my way into software
sections.body:
The repetitive parts of architecture were what first pulled me towards coding. At Mutaa, scripts for schedules and legends saved a working day on each project. I also wrote a script that opened files and sent them to print, with a Telegram notification if the printer failed. I also taught three colleagues to write their own scripts, so automation became something the team could use rather than something only I could do.

For my master's thesis, I worked on bringing Revit building models to the web. That became HAWSR, where architecture and programming came together.

When I joined UNOPS, I kept practising architecture. I still saw myself as an architect while learning to code at nights and weekends. I also built automations for repetitive work there. They continued the pattern I had started at Mutaa, but the work was more involved and required more coding.

That overlap made my move into software gradual. After my UNOPS contract ended, I joined a startup in an engineering role. Software had become the work I wanted to keep doing.

sections.heading: The habits I still use
sections.body: Architecture gave me practical ways to organise work that I still use when building software. A brief and a sketch help me understand the problem before I start. Coordination means agreeing how the different parts fit together, then checking that everyone is building towards the same thing.

items.title: Keep decisions with the work
items.text: At UNOPS, I moved site engineers from phone calls to BIM 360. It cut calls by about 75% and gave everyone a shared place to track issues and decisions. That experience showed me how written, shared channels can keep a team aligned without another meeting.

items.title: Review before it becomes expensive
items.text: I once found a problem 24 hours before a project started and reworked it in time. The potential cost was around $80,000. That experience is a good reason to make time for review, whether I'm looking at a building model or a software change.

unops.name: UNOPS, Anbar
unops.tagline: Coordinating a team on a housing reconstruction program in Anbar.
unops.summary: I worked on the UNOPS reconstruction program for around 1,500 homes in Anbar, helping families displaced by the conflict. I led four architects and six engineers, and coordinated contractors, budgets, schedules and BIM work. It was my final year in construction, while I was already spending nights and weekends writing code.

sections.heading: Rebuilding homes in Anbar
sections.lede: The work was part of a reconstruction program for families displaced by the conflict.
sections.body: From August 2022 to August 2023, I worked as a BIM consultant on the UNOPS housing reconstruction program in Anbar, Iraq. The program covered around 1,500 homes. My responsibilities connected the drawings and models to the contractors, budget and delivery schedule, under the conditions we found on site.

sections.heading: Keeping the team working from the same plan
sections.body: I led four architects and six engineers, alongside the contractors, suppliers and others involved in the program. Each group needed a different kind of support. With the architects, I reviewed drawings and kept a consistent standard. With the engineers, I used a shared model, schedule and list of open issues to coordinate the work.
sections.lede: A model was only useful if it matched the work on site.

sections.heading: What that taught me about leading
sections.body: Keeping the budget and schedule visible helped the team understand what we were working toward. Defining what finished meant for each trade before work started was just as important. I learned to listen to the people doing the building, because they could see problems in a plan that were easy to miss on a screen. Leading the work meant making things clear and following through.

sections.heading: Moving into software
sections.body: I kept writing code at night and on weekends throughout the contract, and joined my first software engineering role at a startup before it ended. I was moving into a different field, but I brought the experience of working with a team, coordinating a plan and taking responsibility for the result. That experience still shapes how I work with engineers today.

mutaa.name: Mutaa Al-Hashimi
mutaa.tagline: A registered Iraqi architecture and engineering consultancy.
mutaa.summary: I joined Mutaa Al-Hashimi as an architect in October 2019 and became Senior Architect before leaving in October 2022. I managed schedules and deliverables for more than 65 projects, designed more than 45, and later led a project team of three architects, six engineers and four foremen through more than twenty projects. Alongside the design work, I started writing scripts to make the repeated work easier. That became an important part of how I worked and taught other architects.

sections.heading: Designing projects and helping the team deliver them
sections.body: My work went beyond producing a design. I managed schedules and deliverables, followed up with architects and engineers, and coordinated the information needed to take projects into construction. As Senior Architect, I led a project team of three architects, six engineers and four foremen through more than twenty projects. The work below includes my designs and contributions to projects at the firm, with my part described where it involved a team.

sections.heading: Making the repeated work easier
sections.body:
I set the firm's first BIM standards, template and guide for design and construction, based on ISO 19650. I also wrote Dynamo scripts to automate schedules and legends. They saved more than a working day per project, and I taught three new colleagues how to use them, improve them and write their own.

The same thinking applied to communication. Moving coordination with site engineers to BIM 360 reduced phone calls by about 75%. I also brought Lumion renders and animations into the final client package. These were practical changes to how the team prepared and shared its work.

sections.heading: Building 188, where design and automation came together
sections.body: Building 188 was one of my first projects at the firm. I designed the office building and produced its detailed drawings, while developing my Revit and Dynamo skills to prepare the drawings faster. As BIM coordinator, I also worked with the other disciplines to reduce clashes in the model.

sections.body: For these chandeliers, I started with concept forms made through scripting, then designed the structure and details of each one. sections.heading: Following residential projects onto site
sections.body:
For Residentials 209, Residential 218 and House 192 in Baghdad, I worked on the design, construction coordination and supervision. The site photos sit alongside the drawings and visualizations because my responsibility continued beyond the model.

Residentials 209 is a three-storey home on 600 sqm. Its classical facade required detailed modelling of the stone and metalwork in Revit so the pieces would fit together. Residential 218 combines a ground-floor home with two apartments above on a 300 sqm plot. Its Shanshool, also known as a Mashrabiya, brings an Iraqi architectural feature into a modern facade. House 192 is a two-storey home on 300 sqm with five bedrooms and four bathrooms, with an entrance designed to be clear from the street.

sections.heading: Different briefs, different residential layouts
sections.body:
The residential work covered very different plots and requirements. Villa 236 had a narrow 400 sqm plot with a 1:4 proportion, yet needed five en-suite bedrooms, eight bathrooms, a waterfall, fountain and panoramic lift. An open plan with an interior courtyard and a bridge to the main bedroom gave the layout room to work.

Residential 235 in Hilla has two matching units joined by a hall for up to seventy people, with a pool and rooftop barbecue area. Villa 232 in Baghdad uses a white diamond-shaped entrance against a mostly grey facade. Villa 201 in Ramadi pairs a simple modern facade with red brick, while Villa 234 in Hilla combines limestone, dark oak and rose gold finishes with a courtyard and double-height reception.

sections.heading: What I carried into software
sections.body: This was where I started writing scripts and helping colleagues use and develop them. Architecture gave me experience coordinating people, schedules and detailed work, while automation gave me another way to solve the repeated problems in front of the team. Both became part of the work I moved into later.

alriyad.name: Al-Riyad Group
alriyad.tagline: Showrooms and a trade-fair booth for Iraq's number one company in power, lighting and electrical control systems.
alriyad.summary: I worked as an architect at Al-Riyad Group from July 2017 to October 2019, designing and supervising four showrooms. The company wanted to update its spaces, so I developed a modular display system that was practical to manufacture, replace and transport. It became the design process used across nine showrooms. I also designed and supervised the company's booth for the Iraq Energy Exhibition in 2018.

stats.label: IEE 2018 booth I designed and supervised

sections.heading: A display system the company could reuse
sections.lede: The old showrooms had lighting fixtures bolted into fixed display boards, leaving visible fixings that were difficult to hide.
sections.body: I replaced that approach with two modular pieces. A background frame provided the structure, while a separate front panel was easy to manufacture and inexpensive to replace. This gave the products a cleaner display and made the system practical to reuse across branches. It became the company's showroom design process and was used in nine locations. The Baghdad main branch shows the full version of the system.

freelance.name: Freelance
freelance.tagline: Designing around the space, budget and plans a client already had.
freelance.summary: Between 2019 and 2021, I worked independently on eight projects for private clients, from houses and small interiors to the presentation of a mall. The work started with what each client needed. Sometimes that meant fitting a family home onto a small plot, sometimes it meant planning for another use later, and sometimes it meant making an existing house work within a budget. These projects show how I turned those constraints into layouts, drawings and visualizations.

sections.heading: A business first, a home later
sections.body:
The client needed specific spaces and dimensions for a business, but wanted the same building to become a house later. I planned both layouts together so the conversion would need as little construction as possible.

The transition happens in phases. Planning that second use from the beginning meant the business layout could meet its own requirements while leaving a practical route to a home. The plans below show both uses and how the building changes between them.

sections.heading: Making a home on 45 sqm

The Tiny House was for a young family of two with a 45 sqm plot. I designed the plan to make full use of that space while leaving room to add another room later if they needed it.

Like the Business House, the layout had to account for the client's needs now and the changes they might make in the future. Here, that meant keeping the possibility of an extra room within a very small plot.

sections.heading: Leaving room for a growing family
sections.body:
The Practical House had a similar brief for a family of four. They wanted to make full use of their plot, including a garage and a spacious guest room.

I planned the guest room so it could later be divided into a smaller guest room and another bedroom. The extra bedroom was a possibility built into the layout, rather than something the family would have to find space for later.

sections.heading: Working with an existing house
sections.body:
Not every client was starting with an empty plot. For this project, the client had just bought a house and wanted to redesign its facade and interiors. The narrow plot and the budget shaped the work, so I used simple elements and materials for the elevation.

Inside, I used light finishes and an open plan to help the main space feel larger. I also fitted as much storage as possible into the kitchen. The facade comparison and interior renders show the proposed changes.

sections.heading: Presenting a mall in Al-Najaf
sections.body:
For the mall, my contribution was its presentation. I produced exterior and interior renders, worked on their post-processing, and made a four-minute 3D animation covering both parts of the building. I edited the animation in Adobe Premiere Pro.

This was a different part of the work from designing a house or an interior. The images and animation brought the spaces together in a presentation, from the site and exterior to the lobby and offices.

school.name: School and BIM
school.tagline: How my architecture studies led me to visual scripting.
school.summary: I studied Architectural Engineering at the University of Technology in Baghdad. My early projects taught me to work through a building's requirements, from the way people move through it to how it fits into the city. I continued learning after graduation, through housing design and BIM. By 2021, I was rebuilding complex geometry in Dynamo and writing my own Grasshopper scripts. These projects show that progression, from designing buildings to experimenting with the tools that create them.

sections.heading: 5 Stars Hotel in Baghdad, 2015
sections.body: This was the first complex project I designed during my undergraduate degree. A hotel brought many functions into one building, so I had to work through its requirements and sections together. I learned to plan vertical circulation, emergency exits and service routes as part of the design. The drawings below show how those decisions came together, from the ground floor to the tower.

sections.heading: Baghdad's Financial Centre, 2017
sections.body: For my graduation project, I proposed redeveloping Baghdad's financial centre on a site beside the Tigris. My concept connected finance and technology through smart office buildings that technology companies could use. It brought the building and urban design work from the earlier projects together in one district, with a master plan, river elevation and sections through the site.

sections.heading: Global Housing Design, 2020
sections.body: After graduation, I continued studying architecture through Global Housing Design, GHD1x on edX from Delft University of Technology. The course looked at housing problems that recur around the world, while recognising that each place needs its own response. My final assignment explored incrementality, a mix of housing types and clustering. The three sheets below take the proposal from its site to the detailed design.

sections.heading: BIMA+ Module 3, 2021
sections.body: In the BIMA+ programme, I started exploring how geometry could be created and changed through visual scripting. For the Module 3 final project, I rebuilt a complex reference, then edited it and tried different ways of producing the same shape. I wanted to deepen my understanding of geometry creation and optimisation while widening my software skills. The work moved from analysing the reference to generative design results, with the full Dynamo graph showing how I built it.

sections.body: After Module 3, I wanted to go further with visual scripting. I knew about Grasshopper but hadn't used it, so I started writing geometric scripts of my own. volunteering.name: Volunteering
volunteering.tagline: Sharing BIM with engineers, planning homes for families, and learning to lead and speak.
volunteering.summary: My volunteer work gave me different ways to use what I knew and learn from other people. I taught BIM to engineers at Iraq's Ministry of Construction and Housing, planned homes for four families through a UAE ministry program, and took part in Startup Weekend and Toastmasters. Some of the work was about architecture, and some was about explaining an idea and bringing people together around it.

sections.heading: Teaching BIM through a house model
sections.body: In August and September 2014, I ran a month of BIM workshops for Iraq's Ministry of Construction and Housing. The participants included engineers who had never used BIM, so I built a sample house they could work through. Its plans, elevations and model gave us something concrete to use when explaining the fundamentals. The workshops introduced BIM to about 1% of the ministry's engineers.

sections.heading: Planning around a family's needs
sections.body: In 2020, I joined an online volunteer program run by the UAE's Ministry of Infrastructure Development. I worked with four families to understand what they needed from a home and what they could afford, then planned their houses around those constraints. The program also brought me four clients in the UAE. One villa consultation had a particularly clear brief. Improve the plan without changing the villa's concept, facade or function, and stay within the client's budget. The original and revised plans below show that work.

sections.heading: Bringing a team around an idea
sections.body: At Startup Weekend Baghdad in 2017, I led a team of seven people with different strengths. We had three days to develop a business model and a working prototype for a digital furniture business using augmented reality. It was a short project, but we had to bring the business idea and the prototype together as one piece of work.

sections.heading: Practising how I explain my work
sections.body: I joined Baghdad Toastmasters Club in February 2018 and continued until October 2021. I completed 11 projects across four levels, spoke to audiences of more than 100 people, and evaluated more than 20 other members. Alongside the design and team work, this gave me regular practice in speaking, listening and giving feedback.
